title: Lantern Night

pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 62. Lantern Festival. Bowls sold: I lost count. Weather: lanterns.*

The clouds snapped open right as the sun hit the horizon. It was not a slow fade. It was a blink. One moment the lane was gray and quiet, the next it was alive with light.

Hundreds of lanterns blinked on, red and gold, hanging in long rivers over the stalls. Some were round, some were shaped like roosters with painted combs. Riddles were pinned to strings of beads, swaying in the warm air. The smell hit me all at once: tangyuan, oyster omelets, burnt sugar, and the deep brown scent of star anise.

I had lived here my whole life. I knew every stall, every step, every crack in the pavement. But standing there, looking up at the glowing shapes, I felt like I was seeing it for the first time. It was a river of light, and we were standing in the middle of it.

A group of children from school ran past, stamp cards in hand, shouting as they chased each other toward the temple. The air was thick and sweet. My apron felt tight. I took a breath. It smelled like home.
pages.image: A night market lane at dusk filled with glowing red and gold paper lanterns hanging overhead, a small girl in a green jacket looking up in wonder at the light and steam rising from stalls below.

pages.text:
The crowd did not arrive all at once. It trickled in, then rushed. Families from the new mall, tourists with cameras, old friends, whole classes. The lane buzzed with voices and the clatter of plastic stools.

At stall nineteen, the line curled around the corner. Ama stood at the pot in her floral vest, her silver curls neat, her towel over one shoulder. She did not look surprised. She looked ready.

I ladled beside her. My hands shook, just a little. Yi-Chen carried bowls with steady hands. Jun ran trays, his spiky hair bouncing. Hui-Ting and her grandmother took the first table. They ordered two bowls of my Lantern Broth.

I watched Hui-Ting’s face as the steam rose. She closed her eyes. My stomach did a nervous flip, the kind that happens before a pop quiz. If she hated it, I would have to hide in the bathroom. But she opened her eyes and smiled.

"Taste first," she said, softly. "Talk later."
pages.image: A busy night market stall with a long line of people, an elderly woman in a floral vest ladling soup, a girl in a checked apron beside her, and two other children carrying bowls and trays.

pages.text:
At eight o'clock, Ms. Xu arrived, wearing sensible shoes and a neat coat that looked like it had been ironed by a very serious person. She walked slowly down the lane, pausing to look at the swaying lanterns, the ring-toss games, and the faces of the people eating. Finally, she stopped at our stall, where the air was thick with the smell of ginger and roasted tomato.

She did not order immediately. Instead, she stood still and watched Ama work, then watched me wipe down the tables, and finally watched the steam rise from the pot in slow, lazy curls. Only then did she sit down at table two, placing her notebook neatly on the surface.

I brought her two bowls. One was Ama’s classic beef noodle soup, rich and dark like a deep pot of ink. The other was my Lantern Broth, clear and golden, filled with shiitake mushrooms and daikon. Ms. Xu tasted the first one, closing her eyes for a brief moment as if she were solving a difficult math problem. Then she tasted the second.

"They are not the same," she said.

"No," I replied. "They are family."

She looked at me, then at Ama. She did not smile, but her eyes were soft, like the light from a paper lantern in a dark room. She took a third sip of the broth and waited.
pages.image: A woman in a neat coat sits at a small table tasting two different bowls of soup while Lin, an eleven-year-old girl with a chin-length black bob and straight bangs, in a dark green padded jacket and a red-and-white checked apron, watches her closely, steam rising between them.

pages.text:
Ms. Xu asked who had taught me. I thought for a second, my mind drifting to the notebook, the measuring spoons, and the failed broths. Then I remembered the river.

"Me," I said. "And Mr. Tsai. And a river."

Ms. Xu smiled. It was a small smile, but it reached her eyes. She opened her notebook and wrote something down. I could not see what it said, but she wrote it carefully, then closed the book.

When she stood up, she did not leave. She turned to Ama, across the steam, and bowed a little. It was a small bow, respectful and warm. Then she said she would have a third bowl.

Ama nodded. She did not speak. She just ladled.

I felt a warm feeling spread through my chest, like hot broth. I had been afraid this would be the end. But it felt like the beginning.
pages.image: A woman bowing slightly to an elderly woman across a steaming pot, a girl in a green jacket watching with a smile, lanterns glowing in the background. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
The night was almost over, and the crowd had thinned until the lane felt more like a long hallway than a market. The lanterns still glowed, but the wind had picked up, pushing the paper shades gently to one side.

Ama took the old brass ladle from my hand. It was dented and heavy, the kind of weight that makes your arm ache, and it belonged to her mother. She held it out to me, palm up, waiting. For the first time in forty years, she stepped back from the pot.

I ladled the last bowl of the night. It was Ama’s classic, with a curl of tangerine peel floating on top like a little orange boat. I handed it to her.

"Chia̍h-pá-buē?" I said.

Ama laughed. It was a bright, happy sound, the kind that makes you want to smile back even if you are tired. "Not yet," she said. "I was waiting for you to ask."

She ate it standing at her own stall, as if it were the first bowl she had ever tasted. I watched her face, then looked at the empty pot. The steam rose, then faded. It was not the end. It was just the next step.
pages.image: An elderly woman eating a bowl of soup standing at a stall, a girl in a green jacket watching her with a smile, a dented brass ladle resting on the counter, soft lantern light around them.
